newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Investors ignore woes, snap up Petrobras.
newsitem.headline: Investors ignore woes, snap up Petrobras.

text.p: Shrugging off dim prospects for privatization and delays in passing Brazil's new Oil Law, investors are snapping up shares of Brazilian state oil monopoly Petrobras, analysts said.
"The market has been receiving positive signals recently and it is taking another look" at Petrobras, said Ricardo Kobayashi, an analyst from local investment bank Banco Pactual.
Undervalued for most of 1996, Petrobras shares have soared in January, far outperforming the hefty overall 10 percent surge in Brazilian stock so far this year, analysts said.
In Friday's session alone, Petrobras preferred was up more than four percent at 200 reais, while its voting common had surged 5.25 percent at 165.50 reais by late afternoon on the Sao Paulo bourse.
Analysts credit Petrobras' rise to investor glee as a result of a surprise fuel increase in December, fresh oil and gas discoveries and a steady drumbeat of good news regarding draft oil legislation.
As a result, many of them are scrambling to reassess the company with an eye toward raising price targets and earnings forecasts.
"I'm maintaining a buy recommendation on the company, but I'll probably be raising my forecasts," said Sidney Chamey of Fator Securities.
"Our projections will be going up," said one analyst at a foreign investment bank in Brazil, who asked that her name not be used. "The trend is very positive right now."
Interest in Petrobras stock waned early in 1996 after the government shelved plans to privatize the firm, analysts said.
That pessimism deepened with slow progress on writing the Oil Law, which would end the state's monopoly of the sector.
"The market was shocked when it realized Petrobras was not going to be privatized when Telebras, (Companhia) Vale do Rio Doce and others were," one analyst said.
But investors began taking another look at Petrobras late last year, when the company announced the discovery of new oil reserves, analysts said.

The new interest bloomed into enthusiasm in December, when the government surprised the market by announcing a fuel rise that would eliminate a $1 billion deficit associated with gasoline and alcohol subsidies, they said.
In January, reports the new Oil Law, which is not expected to be passed by Congress until late 1997, further brightened the outlook for the company.
Analysts said the new legislation might open the company's capital stock to foreign investors.
"If that happens, that would be excellent," said Ana Siquiera, an analyst with local investment bank Banco Icatu.

The new law also is likely to phase out subsidies altogether and allow the company to keep the oil and gas production lots it wants and form joint ventures with private investors to develop others, analysts said.
"That means Petrobras will remain a predominant player in the oil sector and will enable Brazil to more quickly develop its reserves," Kobayashi said.
